title: Why Nvidia's board wouldn't want Jensen Huang to return
excerpt: Jensen Huang's boosters are trying to get Nvidia to reinstate him as CEO, like what happened with Sam Altman in 2023. But there are big differences.
content_html:
Nvidia has plenty of reasons not to bring back Jensen Huang

By Peter Kafka

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Chief Correspondent covering media and technology

2026-11-16T20:02:58.333Z

Sam Altman came back. Can Jensen Huang do it, too?

After all, it was just three years ago when the leader of an enormously important AI company was pushed out by his board, then returned days later after an outcry from employees and Silicon Valley power players.

But Huang in 2026 is not Altman in 2023. That doesn't mean we won't see the same story played out. It does mean it seems less likely: Right now, Nvidia's position is that it's not happening.

To understand why, we need a brief recap:

The story began with China: in 2025, The New York Times reported that federal officials were investigating whether Singapore-based Megaspeed was diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. Last month, the Times reported that officials suspected Megaspeed executive Alice Huang of being a "Chinese intelligence asset" and that she had a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang. The Nvidia CEO and his company dismissed the concerns.

Then it metastasized into a story about Huang's conduct. He acknowledged being unfaithful, and Nvidia said it would investigate whether he had been targeted by foreign intelligence, while expressing support for him. Days later, after the Times alerted Nvidia to a story about Huang's relationship with a direct report, the board met. Huang resigned the next morning.

Since then, reports have described disagreement in Washington over Alice Huang's role, and long-running suspicions of Jensen Huang among China hawks including Marco Rubio. Some of that tension is now public, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling out Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia policy.

And yes, that's the short version of the recap. But it's important to go over it. Because in some narratives — especially the ones promoted by Jensen Huang's vocal supporters — the story is really about Nvidia's foes working to remove a leader they don't like for political reasons.

Perhaps it is! But that's why the timeline is important to underline. Maybe Nvidia's board would have pushed Huang to resign if the issue was solely about his relationship to Alice Huang, and/or the way Nvidia chips have been used by China.

Last week's newsflow, though, suggests that it was news of the affair with Jensen Huang's employee that pushed the board to ultimately act.

So there's a version of a story where Nvidia's board may not have pushed out its visionary leader if the only issue was China. Disclosure of the second affair (Reuters has subsequently reported yet another affair with another Nvidia employee) is what did it.

All of which makes bringing Huang back more complicated than Altman's story.

In Altman's case, OpenAI's board was unable to clearly tell a story about why, exactly, they fired Altman. In Huang's case, Nvidia's board can point to multiple instances where Huang reportedly violated his own company's rules. It can also argue that Huang misled his own company about his behavior, as multiple outlets have reported. Those are all fireable offenses in most of corporate America, regardless of national security debates.

In the inevitable shareholder lawsuits that will follow Huang's departure (one has already been filed), board members will be criticized for not uncovering Huang's acts on their own. They will be able to say, credibly, that once the acts came to light, they acted, which led to Huang's ouster.

But bringing Huang back once those facts are known will generate much more risk for the board: Board members couldn't simply say that Huang was the victim of a political plot. They'd have to explain why they thought his transgressions weren't harming the company. And if Nvidia stock fell for any reason after Huang came back, they would face blowback for that, too.

What about the fact Huang has boosters throughout Silicon Valley, and in the White House? Donald Trump had reportedly told Huang not to resign last week, and on Monday said he "wouldn't mind" if Huang came back.

Perhaps if this were a couple of years ago, after Trump's victory in what was described as a vibe-shift election, Nvidia officials and board members might agree to follow Trump's lead.

And they might have expected some kind of political or legal shield for their actions — like the kind that Apple and Google got from the Trump administration when they agreed to keep hosting TikTok in America, contrary to US law.

But this time around it's not really clear what the White House position actually is on Huang and Nvidia. Trump has spoken glowingly about Huang and Nvidia, but that's different than pushing a private company to reinstate a disgraced CEO.

Meanwhile, the Democrats have won their own supposed vibe shift election, and have promised to spend the next couple years investigating both Trump and his private sector allies. Bringing Huang back at Trump's behest makes Nvidia and its board even bigger targets. That alone may be enough to keep him out of the company for good.
